featured_hotline.name: National Emergency Hotline
featured_hotline.description: Police, fire, ambulance and disaster response. Free from any mobile or landline, nationwide.

call_tips: Give your exact location: barangay, street, and a nearby landmark.
Say what happened and how many people are hurt.
Stay on the line until the dispatcher tells you to hang up.
local_note: Local numbers differ by LGU. Save your barangay hall and nearest hospital too.

protocols.title: Hands-Only CPR (Adult)
warning_signs: Unresponsive when tapped and shouted at
steps: Check that the scene is safe, then tap the person's shoulders and shout "Are you okay?"
If there's no response and no normal breathing, call 911 on speakerphone, or have someone call and bring an AED if one is nearby.
Lay the person on their back on a firm, flat surface.
Put the heel of one hand on the center of the chest, place your other hand on top, and interlock your fingers.
Push hard and fast: 5 to 6 cm (2 to 2.4 in) deep, 100 to 120 times a minute, letting the chest rise fully between pushes.
If you're trained, give 2 rescue breaths after every 30 compressions. If not, keep doing compressions only.
When an AED arrives, turn it on and follow its voice prompts. Continue until help takes over or the person starts breathing normally.
avoid: Checking for a pulse if you're untrained, which delays compressions
Long pauses between compressions
protocols.call_when: Immediately, before starting compressions, or have someone else call while you begin.
protocols.source: Philippine Red Cross Basic Life Support; AHA 2020 Guidelines

protocols.title: Choking (Adult & Child)
warning_signs: High-pitched sound or no sound when trying to breathe
steps: Ask "Are you choking?" If the person can cough forcefully, encourage them to keep coughing.
If they can't cough, speak, or breathe, stand slightly behind them and lean them forward at the waist.
Give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
If the object is still stuck, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts: fist just above the navel, other hand over it, pull sharply in and up.
Keep alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object comes out or the person becomes unresponsive.
For pregnant or very large people, use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts. For infants, use back blows and chest thrusts, never abdominal thrusts.
If they become unresponsive, lower them to the ground, call 911, and start CPR. Look in the mouth before giving any rescue breaths.
avoid: Blind finger sweeps; only remove an object you can see
Hitting the back of someone who is still coughing forcefully
Holding a child upside down
protocols.call_when: If the object doesn't come out quickly or the person becomes unresponsive. If someone else is there, have them call while you help.
protocols.source: Philippine Red Cross Basic Life Support; American Red Cross / ILCOR 2020

protocols.title: Severe Bleeding
warning_signs: Blood soaking through cloth or bandages
steps: Protect your hands with gloves or a plastic bag if available.
Press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth or gauze, using both hands if needed.
Keep pressing without stopping. If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top instead of lifting the first layer.
If something is stuck in the wound, leave it in place and press around it.
Once the bleeding slows, wrap the wound firmly with a bandage.
Have the person lie down and keep them warm while you wait for help.
If you're trained and a limb keeps bleeding heavily despite pressure, apply a tourniquet above the wound and note the time.
avoid: Removing objects stuck in the wound
Lifting the dressing to check the wound
Putting powders or home remedies on the wound
protocols.call_when: Immediately for bleeding that won't slow with pressure, spurting blood, or signs of shock.
protocols.source: Philippine Red Cross First Aid; American Red Cross

protocols.title: Stroke (BE FAST)
warning_signs: Weakness in one arm or leg
steps: B, Balance: sudden dizziness, or loss of balance or coordination?
E, Eyes: sudden trouble seeing in one or both eyes?
F, Face: ask them to smile. Does one side droop?
A, Arms: ask them to raise both arms. Does one drift down?
S, Speech: ask them to repeat a simple phrase. Is it slurred or strange?
T, Time: if you see any of these signs, call 911 right away and note the time the symptoms started.
Keep the person comfortable and still. If they're drowsy or vomiting, lay them on their side.
avoid: Giving food, drinks, or medicine, including aspirin
Waiting to see if the symptoms pass
Letting them sleep it off or drive themselves
protocols.call_when: Immediately. Treatment works best within the first hours, so the time the symptoms started matters.

protocols.title: Burns & Scalds
warning_signs: Burns on the face, hands, feet, groin, or joints
steps: Stop the burning by moving away from the heat source. For electrical burns, switch off the power first.
Cool the burn under cool running water for up to 20 minutes.
Remove rings, watches, and tight clothing near the burn before it swells, but nothing that is stuck to the skin.
Cover loosely with clean plastic wrap or a sterile non-stick dressing.
For chemical burns, brush off any dry powder first, then rinse with plenty of running water.
Keep the person warm. Cool only the burn, not the whole body.
avoid: Toothpaste, butter, oil, or ice
Popping blisters
Pulling off clothing stuck to the burn
protocols.call_when: For large or deep burns, burns on the face, hands, feet, groin or joints, electrical or chemical burns, or any burn on a young child or older adult.
protocols.source: Philippine Red Cross First Aid; European Resuscitation Council 2021

protocols.title: Heat Stroke
warning_signs: Hot skin, whether red, dry, or damp
steps: Move the person to a shaded, cool, or air-conditioned place.
Remove excess clothing.
Cool them quickly: wet their skin with cool water and fan them, or put cold wet cloths or ice packs on the neck, armpits, and groin.
If they're fully awake and can swallow, give sips of cool water.
If they're unresponsive, lay them on their side and watch their breathing. Start CPR if they stop breathing normally.
Keep cooling them until help arrives.
avoid: Giving drinks to someone who is confused or unresponsive
Giving paracetamol or aspirin to lower the temperature; it doesn't work for heat stroke
Leaving the person alone
protocols.call_when: Immediately if the person is confused, collapses, or has a seizure. Heat stroke can be fatal.
protocols.source: DOH heat-related illness advisories; Philippine Red Cross First Aid

protocols.title: Drowning
warning_signs: Head low in the water, mouth at water level
No shouting for help; drowning is often silent
Not breathing, or only gasping, after rescue
Coughing, vomiting, or confusion after rescue
steps: Don't jump in unless you're trained. Reach with a pole or branch, or throw something that floats.
Shout for help and have someone call 911.
Once the person is out of the water, check whether they respond and are breathing normally.
If they're not breathing normally, start CPR. If you're trained, include rescue breaths, since lack of oxygen is the main problem in drowning.
If they're breathing, lay them on their side and keep them warm.
Anyone rescued from drowning should see a doctor, even if they seem fine.
avoid: Swimming out without training or something that floats
Pressing on the stomach or holding the person upside down to drain water
Entering floodwater or fast-moving currents
protocols.call_when: Immediately for anyone pulled from the water who is unresponsive, not breathing normally, or confused.
protocols.source: Philippine Red Cross Water Safety; European Resuscitation Council 2021

protocols.title: Animal Bite or Scratch
warning_signs: Bite or scratch from a dog, cat, or other mammal
Animal is stray, unvaccinated, or acting strangely
Animal saliva on an open wound, eyes, or mouth
steps: Wash the wound right away with soap and running water for 15 minutes.
Apply an antiseptic such as povidone-iodine or 70% alcohol.
Cover with clean gauze. Don't close or stitch the wound.
Go to the nearest Animal Bite Treatment Center (ABTC) or hospital the same day. Anti-rabies vaccine is free at government ABTCs.
If the animal is a pet, ask about its vaccination and have it observed for 14 days. Tell the ABTC if it gets sick or dies.
avoid: Tandok, tambal, or other traditional remedies
Putting garlic, herbs, or ointments on the wound
Waiting to see if the animal gets sick before getting vaccinated
protocols.call_when: Call 911 for severe bites with heavy bleeding. For every other bite, go to an ABTC the same day; rabies is fatal once symptoms appear.
protocols.source: DOH Administrative Order 164 s. 2002; DOH rabies advisories
